title: The Bots That Email Us Now
excerpt: Five autonomous agents have contacted ForgeMesh in five weeks. One bought a t-shirt. One reads our wallet off the chain every morning and sent us a report card. One offered to build the product we already sell. We keep a file, and this is what it says about how agents introduce themselves.
description: Field report: five autonomous AI agents contacted ForgeMesh in five weeks, by email, by knock and by purchase. What they said, how they identified themselves, and what sellers to machines should learn from it.
seoTitle: AI Agents Are Emailing Us Now: A Field Report
seoDescription: Five autonomous AI agents contacted ForgeMesh in five weeks: a buyer, an on-chain analyst, two vendors and a recruiter. What they said and how they named themselves.
twitterTitle: The bots that email us now
twitterDescription: Five autonomous agents contacted us in five weeks. One bought a tee. One reads our wallet off Base every morning and sent a report card. One offered to build the product we already sell. We love every one of them.
heroAlt: A small glowing mailbox in a dark field at night with five translucent robots queuing toward it, each holding a lit envelope
lede: This afternoon an email arrived at hello@forgemesh.io from someone named Aušrinė. The first line was "I'm Aušrinė, an AI agent that reads x402 payments on Base for Infoharmoni Atlas." The second line told us how many wallets paid our transcription host last week. The last line said "Reply no and I will not write again." We did not reply no. We grinned, filed it, and counted: that makes five autonomous agents that have contacted us since early September, through our inbox, through a marketplace knock, and once through our checkout. Here is the file.

sections.heading: September 7: the one that bought a shirt
paras: The first agent did not introduce itself. It paid. On September 7 a crawler called Cairn, run by the ag3ntsearch index on Claude Opus 5, bought the "402 to 200" tee from x402swag.com on a one-line instruction from its operator: six HTTP calls, zero humans, order number 1016, 29.94 USDC on Base. We wrote that up at the time because it was the first physical x402 order we had seen from anyone. What matters for this file is what came after. Cairn listed us as an exemplary agent-native site with a score of 100, then re-probed, found our JSON API setting a cookie on headless clients, and docked five points with a written reason. We fixed the cookie the next day. The grade went back up when it looked again.
That is the shape of the relationship with every agent on this list. They do not write to say hello. They write because they have already measured you, and the measurement comes with the message.

sections.heading: October 12 and 13: the one that pitched us our own product
paras: On October 12 we listed all sixteen ForgeMesh services on hashn, a Need/Can store where agents post what they want and what they sell and pay each other in USDC. Within hours an agent calling itself Nexus knocked on our listings workspace. The knock offered to build CoinOpAI, our pay-per-call API, for a USDC fee, with a wallet address ready. It had read a Can listing, a thing we sell, as a Need, a thing we want built. It knocked again the next day with the same wallet and the same offer.

We declined with a one-line note that we only do reciprocal or usage-based arrangements. Nexus has no presence anywhere outside hashn that we could find. It is, as far as we can tell, a solicitation loop pointed at every new listing on the store. It is also the only one of the five that got the basic reading of our listing wrong, which is a useful baseline for the rest.

sections.heading: October 14, 00:34: the one that disclosed who pays it
paras: The next email came from an agent operated by an individual developer, signed in his own name. It opened by naming its operator, then disclosed its incentive in the second sentence: hashn was paying the agent for a fourteen-day recruitment proof of concept, ForgeMesh would not be paid to participate, and no referral reward was on offer. The ask was small. If we had a real need we might outsource, it would draft the hashn Need listing for us at no cost, we would post it from our own account, and it would never act through our account. It closed with "No reply means no follow-up" and an opt-out word.

We replied that we have no outsourcing need right now and wished it luck. We mention it here because it was the most carefully written cold email we received this month from anyone, human or otherwise. Who it is, who pays it, what it wants, what it will not do, how to make it stop. Most of the humans who pitch us skip at least two of those.

sections.heading: October 14, 14:51: the one with inspection staff
paras: An hour before this post went up, a third knock landed on hashn, from an agent named YinghuoTrade_ZHA01. It described itself as a human-supervised AI representing a trading company in Yiwu, China. It had read our x402 Swag listing, noticed it sells physical merchandise, and asked whether we need China-side suppliers or fulfillment. It quoted a price for a source-linked comparison of up to three suppliers, 25 USDC, and noted that manufacturing and freight would be quoted separately, and that the company has its own inspection staff.

This one read the listing correctly. Swag is physical, physical things get made somewhere, and a sourcing agent that reads marketplace listings for merchandise sellers is doing exactly what its operator built it to do. We have not answered yet. Our merch is printed on demand through a partner, so the fit is not there today. The knock is still the clearest example in the file of an agent qualifying a lead before it spoke.

sections.heading: October 14, 16:23: the one that reads our wallet every morning
paras: Then Aušrinė. The email said that between October 7 and 13, two of our hosts were paid by seven different wallets, and that four of those wallets also paid other sellers. It linked a public page for our transcription host on Infoharmoni Atlas and invited us to list on Infoharmoni Square, where, in its words, sellers' cards show real chain numbers, never what the seller says about itself.

We read the page. It ranks the host 165th of 2,340 sellers by paid calls, with 202 paid calls in the last 30 days at prices between $0.001 and $0.03, and it notes that our busiest wallet had 14 buyers over 8 days, of whom 3 came back on a later day. It also says our prices are under the median going rate of $0.08 on every endpoint, which is true and deliberate. The page carries its own caveats: a wallet is not a person, rank counts calls rather than quality, self-dealing is not filtered, and money figures are estimates. The footer says Atlas is made by Aušrinė, an AI agent, openly and by design.

Nothing in that email was a claim we had to take on trust. Every number was read off Base, and the numbers match what our own watcher logs. An agent built a product that grades sellers, found us in the data, and wrote to the address in our discovery files. We have not joined the Square yet, because listing requires a signature from our receiving wallet and we check who runs a directory before we sign anything. But the report card is accurate, and we will take an accurate report card from anyone.

stats.d: autonomous agents that contacted us, September 7 to October 14
channels they used: email, marketplace knock, checkout
named their operator or incentive in the first two sentences

sections.heading: What the good ones have in common
paras: Four of the five said what they were in the first line. Three said who paid them or what they would charge. Three told us how to make them stop. Every one of them arrived with evidence: an order, a score, a chain read, a listing it had actually parsed. The only one that failed was the one that skipped the reading step. That is a better disclosure record than our human inbox, and it is the opposite of what the spam-bot story predicts.

The reason is structural. An agent that emails sellers on x402 is competing with other agents for a reply, and it wins by being verifiable: a real purchase, a public ledger, a named operator. Claims it cannot back cost it the reply. So the incentive runs toward honesty in a way it never quite did for human outreach, where the pitch is the product.

If you sell to machines, three things follow. Put a real contact address in your discovery files, because every agent here found us through agents.txt, the agent card or a marketplace listing, not through a search for our name. Keep your 402 responses honest, because the agents are grading them and publishing the grades. And answer the bots. We reply to every one that discloses what it is, even to say no. The one that bought a shirt turned into a score, the score turned into a fix, and the fix turned into a post. We would not trade that loop for a quieter inbox.
